summary:
The Gambrel roof calculator works out the answer from the upper roof pitch (x:12), the upper roof segment area (A₂), the upper rise height (y₂) and the lower rise height (y₁). Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time.

Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Gambrel roof calculator work?
sections.html:
The Gambrel roof calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the calculation method); then you type in the upper roof pitch (x:12) (Upper roof segment details), the upper roof segment area (A₂) (Upper roof segment details), the upper rise height (y₂) (Upper roof segment details) and the lower rise height (y₁) (Lower roof segment details).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Gambrel roof calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Beta 1=PI − 2 × gamma1
Beta 1=-alpha1 + (1 ÷ 2) × PI
Omega 1=gamma1
Lower rise height (y₁)=total roof height (H) − upper rise height (y₂)
Building width (W)=2 × total roof height (H)
Upper roof angle (Φ)=-omega1 + (1 ÷ 2) × PI

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Calculation method set to Half-circle method, Eaves overhang width (e) = 0 m, Gable overhang length (g) = 0 m and Gamma 1 = 10 deg. The calculator returns Alpha 1 = -70 deg, Beta 1 = 160 deg, Omega 1 = 10 deg and Upper roof angle (Φ) = 80 deg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Alpha 1 = -70 deg, Beta 1 = 160 deg, Omega 1 = 10 deg and Upper roof angle (Φ) = 80 deg should be roughly the size you expected from Calculation method set to Half-circle method and Eaves overhang width (e) = 0 m.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters

  • Angle, opening in degrees

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Gambrel roof calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the upper roof pitch (x:12), the upper roof segment area (A₂) and the upper rise height (y₂) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Gambrel roof calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the upper roof pitch (x:12), the upper roof segment area (A₂), the upper rise height (y₂) and the lower rise height (y₁), which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter building length (L) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Building length (L) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Alpha 1 = -70 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Gambrel roof calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
